Question_text: A student measures the resistance R of a lamp for different values of the potential difference V across it. The student connects the circuit shown in Fig. 1.1. The student: closes the switch, connects the crocodile clip at a length l = 10.0 cm of the resistance wire, records the potential difference V across the lamp, records the current I in the lamp, opens the switch. Fig. 1.2 shows the readings on the voltmeter and the ammeter. The student repeats the procedure with different lengths l of the resistance wire, and the results are shown in Table 1.1.
image: Fig. 1.1 shows an electrical circuit diagram. It consists of a power supply, a resistance wire placed above a metre rule, and a crocodile clip connected to the resistance wire. A lamp (represented by a circle with a cross) is connected in series with the resistance wire, an ammeter (A) is also in series, and a voltmeter (V) is connected in parallel across the lamp. The length 'l' of the resistance wire from one end to the crocodile clip is indicated. Fig. 1.2 shows two analogue meters: a voltmeter and an ammeter. The voltmeter has a scale from 0 to 1.0 V, with a needle pointing to 0.5 V. The ammeter has a scale from 0 to 1.0 A, with a needle pointing to 0.1 A.

Parts.part_text: Record in Table 1.1 the values of V and I. Table 1.1 shows columns for length l/cm, potential difference V/V, current I/A, and resistance R/Ω. The first row for l = 10.0 cm has blank entries for V and I, which need to be recorded from Fig. 1.2. Other rows (l = 30.0, 50.0, 70.0, 90.0, 100.0 cm) have pre-filled data for V, I, and R, with the I value for l = 100.0 cm missing.
Complete the top row of Table 1.1 by calculating the resistance R of the lamp when l = 10.0 cm. Use the equation shown. R = V/I
The student forgets to write in the current value for l = 100.0 cm. Calculate the current and write its value in Table 1.1.

The student examines Table 1.1 and states that the resistance R of the lamp is directly proportional to the length l. State if you agree with the student's statement. Justify your answer by using values from Table 1.1.
On the grid provided in Fig. 1.3, plot a graph of R on the y-axis against V on the x-axis. Start both axes from the origin (0, 0). Draw a smooth curve of best fit.
Parts.image: Fig. 1.3 shows a blank grid with horizontal and vertical axes, labeled 0 at the bottom-left corner, indicating the origin (0,0) for plotting a graph.

Parts.part_text: Using your graph, describe how the resistance R of the lamp changes as the potential difference V across it changes.

Another student makes changes to the circuit shown in Fig. 1.1. She uses a variable resistor to vary the current and potential difference, instead of the resistance wire and the crocodile clip. Complete the circuit diagram in Fig. 1.4 to show how this is done.
Parts.image: Fig. 1.4 shows an incomplete electrical circuit diagram. It includes a voltmeter (V) connected in parallel across a lamp (represented by a circle with a cross), and an ammeter (A) in series with the lamp. The rest of the circuit, including the power supply and the variable resistor, is missing and needs to be completed.

Question_text: A student determines the acceleration of free-fall by timing the oscillations of a pendulum. The pendulum is shown in Fig. 2.1.
image: Fig. 2.1 shows a diagram of a simple pendulum. A stand with a clamp holds a string from which a bob is suspended. A ruler-like scale is shown alongside the string, indicating a measurement for the length 'l' of the pendulum, from the clamp to the center of the bob. The entire setup is drawn to one-eighth actual size.

Parts.part_text: On Fig. 2.1, measure the length l of the pendulum in centimetres to the nearest millimetre.
Fig. 2.1 is drawn one-eighth actual size. Length L is the actual length of the pendulum. Calculate L.
The student gives the bob a small displacement and releases it so that it swings backwards and forwards. Fig. 2.2 shows one complete oscillation of the pendulum.
Parts.image: Fig. 2.2 shows a pendulum bob swinging. It depicts the bob moving from its starting displaced position, through the equilibrium point, to the other extreme displaced position, and then returning to the starting position, illustrating one complete oscillation. A clamp and a string are also visible.

Parts.part_text: The student measures the time t for 20 complete oscillations. The time t is shown on the stop-watch in Fig. 2.3. Write down the time t.
Parts.image: Fig. 2.3 shows a digital stop-watch display. The display reads '00:21.2 min sec', indicating a time of 21.2 seconds.

Parts.part_text: The student measures the time t for 20 oscillations twice more. These times are shown: 21.30 s, 21.28 s. Find the average time tAV for 20 oscillations of the pendulum.
The period T is the time for one complete oscillation of the pendulum. Calculate T.
Calculate a value for g, the acceleration of free-fall. Use the equation shown. g = 11.1 / T^2. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
To find the period T of the pendulum, the student first measures the average time for 20 oscillations. Suggest why the student did not choose to measure the average time for: 2 oscillations
200 oscillations.

Question_text: A student uses a ray box to investigate the refraction of a ray of red light as it passes through a semi-circular glass block. He sets up the apparatus on a sheet of paper as shown in Fig. 3.1.
image: Fig. 3.1 shows a ray box emitting a ray of light, which passes through a red filter, and then is incident on a semi-circular glass block placed on a sheet of paper. The ray hits the flat surface of the block at point M, which is the mid-point. A normal line is drawn perpendicular to the flat surface at M. The angle of incidence 'i' is indicated between the incident ray and the normal. The diagram is for an experiment to investigate refraction.

Parts.part_text: Measure the angle of incidence i of the ray at point M.
The angle of refraction at M is 22°. On Fig. 3.1: draw the refracted ray inside the glass block
label with the letter N, the point where the refracted ray leaves the glass block.
The ray emerges from the glass block at N without further deviation. Draw the path of the ray after it leaves the glass block.
Describe how the student uses optics pins to mark the path of the ray accurately.

Question_text: A student uses a thermometer to measure the temperature of hot water as it cools down in a beaker. Explain why he takes the following steps to ensure that the values are accurate.

Parts.part_text: He makes sure that the thermometer bulb does not touch the sides or the base of the beaker.
He stirs the water each time before taking a reading.
He takes the temperature reading by viewing the scale on the thermometer at eye level, perpendicular to the scale.
